sections.b: Some Corinthians said, "We all have knowledge": an idol is nothing, so the meat is just meat. Paul agrees with the creed (one God, one Lord, 8:4-6) but says love limits how knowledge is used. A believer who eats in an idol's temple may lead a weaker believer to act against conscience, and so "destroy" a brother for whom Christ died (8:11). Paul would give up meat altogether (8:13). Chapter 10 gives the rules for the market and the temple.

common: Paul allows food bought in the market (10:25) but forbids sharing in the table of demons (10:21).
uncommon: Some scholars think chapter 8 allows temple meals and chapter 10 was written to reverse that.

sections.h: The man with his father's wife (1 Corinthians 5)
sections.b: Paul tells the Corinthians to gather and put out a man who is living with his father's wife, handing him over to Satan "for the ruin of his flesh, so that on the day of the Lord his spirit may be saved." The picture is Passover yeast: a little spreads through the dough. He limits the rule to a person who is called a brother or sister, forbids even eating with such a person, and leaves the judgment of outsiders to God (5:12-13). Later churches took this as the base of the ban, excommunication and shunning.

These chapters show the city: lawsuits where honor was won and lost, prostitution and banquets that ended with it, temple dining rooms where meat was eaten, and a mixed church of slaves, free people and a few well-off households. Paul's rulings are local answers: to a case reported to him (5:1), a pattern of lawsuits (6:1), the church's own letter (7:1) and a question about food (8:1). The letter shows a church still shaped by its city's values.

sections.h: Marriage, divorce and the Corinthian letter (1 Corinthians 7)
sections.b: Paul gives marriage equal, mutual rights (7:3-4), passes on the Lord's command that a wife not separate and a husband not divorce his wife (7:10-11), and gives his own ruling that a believer should not divorce an unbelieving spouse who agrees to stay (7:12-13). If the unbeliever leaves, the believer is "not enslaved" (7:15). The churches draw different laws from this: Catholic indissolubility with the Pauline privilege, Protestant grounds of adultery and desertion, Orthodox economy. A widow may marry "only in the Lord" (7:39).

common: Paul separates the Lord's command (7:10) from his own judgment (7:12).
uncommon: David Instone-Brewer reads 7:3-5 and 7:15 against the Jewish background of Exodus 21:10-11 as allowing divorce for neglect.

sections.b: Paul wishes that all were as he is (7:7) and calls singleness and marriage each a gift. He advises the unmarried and widows to stay as they are, but says marriage is not a sin (7:28, 36). His reasons are the "pressure of the present time" (7:26), the shortened time (7:29) and undivided devotion to the Lord (7:35). The Catholic and Orthodox churches honor consecrated virginity and clerical celibacy; the Reformers answered that few have the gift.

Paul uses slavery for the believer's new status: "you were bought, and a price was paid" (6:20; 7:23). To slaves in the church he says not to let it worry them, but if they can become free, to "make use of it instead" (7:21), where the Greek does not say what to use, freedom or slavery. The slave called in the Lord is the Lord's freed person; the free person is Christ's slave (7:22). Readers have disagreed since the early church about what Paul advised.

common: Most modern translations take 7:21 to mean "take the chance to be free."
uncommon: S. Scott Bartchy (1973) argued that the Greek means "use your slavery" instead.

sections.b: Paul uses the word in 5:1 of the man and his father's wife, in 5:9-11 and 6:9 in lists, in 6:13, 18 of the body, and in 7:2 as the reason to marry. It is a wide word. In 6:12-20 he gives a reason of his own: the body belongs to the Lord, so joining it to a prostitute makes it one body with her.

sections.h: Soft men and men who lie with males (1 Corinthians 6:9)
sections.b: Paul's list of those who will not inherit the kingdom contains two words, malakoi ("soft") and arsenokoitai ("male-bedders"). The second is first found here and in 1 Timothy 1:10, and probably draws on the Greek of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13. Traditional readers take the pair to cover same-sex intercourse; others (Boswell, Scroggs, Martin) argue for male prostitution, pederasty or exploitation. The churches' teachings differ (see the card). Paul adds: "And some of you were like this. But you were washed."
sections.refs: 1 Corinthians 6:9; 1 Corinthians 6:10; 1 Corinthians 6:11; 1 Timothy 1:10; Leviticus 18:22; Leviticus 20:13

common: Most commentators think arsenokoitai echoes Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13.
uncommon: Dale Martin argues that the word named economic exploitation, not a kind of sexual act.

sections.h: The Spirit and the body (1 Corinthians 6)
sections.b: Paul calls the believer's body "a temple of the Holy Spirit within you" (6:19), whom "you have from God." To be joined to the Lord is to be "one spirit" with him (6:17). The Spirit is also the means of the change in 6:11: "you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus and in the Spirit of our God." In 7:40 Paul says he thinks he has God's Spirit too.

In 3:16 the church is God's temple; in 6:19 the believer's body is a temple of the Holy Spirit. The Greek is naos, the inner shrine of a temple. The point is not that the body is sacred in itself but that the Spirit lives in it, and that God bought it. Interpreters differ on whether Paul means each person's body or the body of the church.

Paul uses the feast of Unleavened Bread as a picture: the church must clear out the old yeast of malice and evil because "our Passover, Christ, has been slaughtered." It is one of the earliest texts that calls Christ the Passover. The Roman rite reads the passage on Easter Sunday.

sections.h: One God, many so-called gods (1 Corinthians 8:4-6)
sections.b: "An idol is nothing in the world" and "there is no God but one" (8:4) repeat Israel's creed. Paul concedes that there are "so-called gods" and "many lords" (8:5) and then restates the creed: one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ (8:6). Most scholars see this as including Jesus within the one God, not adding a second; some see Wisdom language, and Jewish readers disagree on whether it stays within monotheism. In 10:20 Paul adds that idol sacrifices are offered to demons.

The Greek of Deuteronomy 6:4 says "the Lord our God, the Lord is one." Paul gives "God" to the Father and "Lord" to Jesus: "one God, the Father ... and one Lord, Jesus Christ." The old confession becomes a two-part confession, with the Father as source ("from whom") and Jesus as agent ("through whom") of all things.

sections.h: Idols that are nothing, and demons (1 Corinthians 8:4; 10:20)
sections.b: Paul calls an idol "nothing in the world" (8:4) and later says idol sacrifices are offered to demons (10:20). The Old Testament holds both thoughts: the idol is empty (Psalm 96:5; Isaiah 41:24), yet Deuteronomy 32:17 says the people sacrificed to demons. Paul's answer in chapter 8 turns on the effect on others, not on the idol's power.

sections.h: The body will be raised (1 Corinthians 6:14)
sections.b: "God both raised the Lord and will raise us up through his power." Paul uses the resurrection as an argument about the body in the middle of a discussion of sexual sin: what God will raise is not for a prostitute. The same hope returns at length in chapter 15.

A Jew called by God should not try to undo circumcision, and a Gentile should not be circumcised. "Being circumcised is nothing, and being uncircumcised is nothing. What matters is keeping God's commands." The sentence is central to the "Paul within Judaism" reading, in which Paul expects Jews who believe to remain Jews and Gentiles to remain Gentiles.

sections.h: Washed, and the holiness of children (1 Corinthians 6:11; 7:14)
sections.b: "You were washed" in 6:11 is probably baptism, in a verb that can mean "you washed yourselves" or "had yourselves washed." In 7:14 the unbelieving spouse is "made holy" and the children are "holy"; churches that baptize infants and churches that baptize believers read the line differently.

Paul tells the church to hand the offender "over to Satan for the ruin of his flesh" (5:5), and warns that Satan may tempt a couple who stop sex without agreement (7:5). Satan is the tester who works outside the church and can be used, in God's purpose, for rescue.

"Do you not know that we will judge angels?" Paul assumes that God's people will share in the final judgment, even of angels, probably the rebel angels, as in Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4. He uses it as an argument from the greater to the lesser, against Corinthian lawsuits.

Paul says that "the time has been cut short" and that "the shape of this world is passing away." From this he draws five "as if not" lines: those with wives as if they had none, those who weep as if not weeping, and so on. He does not give a date, and he does not tell married people to leave their marriages, but to hold everything lightly.

In 8:7-12 Paul uses syneidēsis three times (8:7, 10, 12), and eight times in chapters 8 to 10 together: the weak conscience is "stained" when a person eats idol food believing it is a sacrifice, and when a stronger believer leads a weaker one to act against his conscience, he "wounds" it and so sins against Christ. Paul never says the weak conscience is right; he says it must not be pushed.

sections.h: The Shema and the Son (1 Corinthians 8:6)
sections.b: "There is one God, the Father ... and one Lord, Jesus Christ." The Nicene Creed uses the words, and the churches read them differently: as the base of the confession that the Son is of one being with the Father, or, among Unitarians and Jehovah's Witnesses, as distinguishing the one God from his agent Jesus.

sections.h: "A brother for whom Christ died" (1 Corinthians 8:11)
sections.b: Paul says the weak person is "being destroyed" by the knowledge of the strong. Wesleyan and Catholic readers take it as proof that a believer can be lost; Reformed and Baptist readers take it as a warning about what the act would do, or about someone who only seemed to be a believer.

sections.h: Food does not bring us before God (1 Corinthians 8:8)
sections.b: "Food will not bring us before God. If we eat, we do not have more. If we do not eat, we do not have less." Paul's view agrees with Romans 14:14, that nothing is unclean in itself. Yet the same freedom is limited by love for the weak (8:9-13).

"Being circumcised is nothing, and being uncircumcised is nothing. What matters is keeping God's commands." Interpreters differ on which commands: the moral law, the commands of Christ, or, for Jews, the whole Torah (the "Paul within Judaism" view).

sections.h: Who will inherit the kingdom (1 Corinthians 6:9-10)
sections.b: Paul lists ten kinds of wrongdoing and says such people "will not inherit the kingdom of God," then adds that some of the Corinthians once were such, "but you were washed." The kingdom is an inheritance, and a life ruled by these things is not its life.

Paul tells the unmarried and the widows that it is good to stay as he is, but that if they cannot control themselves they should marry (7:8-9). A widow is bound to her husband as long as he lives, and after that is free to marry "only in the Lord" (7:39). He thinks she is "more blessed" if she stays as she is (7:40).

Paul separates three kinds of teaching: the Lord's command (7:10), his own ruling (7:12), and his judgment (7:25, 40). He does not say the second and third bind less, since he gives them "in all the churches" (7:17) and thinks he has God's Spirit (7:40). Whether he was married is not known; he says he wishes all were as he is (7:7).
sections.refs: 1 Corinthians 7:7; 1 Corinthians 7:10; 1 Corinthians 7:12; 1 Corinthians 7:17; 1 Corinthians 7:25; 1 Corinthians 7:40

sections.b: "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up." Paul tests all use of freedom by what builds up another person (8:1; 10:23; 14:3-5). In 8:3 the person who loves God is the one known by God.

sections.h: The authority of Paul's own judgment (1 Corinthians 7)
sections.b: Paul writes "I and not the Lord" (7:12) and "I think I also have God's Spirit" (7:40). The churches on this site all receive Paul's letters as Scripture (for Catholic teaching see Dei Verbum 11), so this is not a point where they divide; they differ on how apostolic teaching is handed on and weighed. The line shows that Paul separated Jesus' sayings from his own judgment while claiming the Spirit's guidance.
